items.sourceTitle: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine

source_propositions.source_text: Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.
Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg.
He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".
Both he and his country have denied any involvement.
It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.
Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.
Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.
The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.

source_propositions.source_text: Syria's Permanent Representative to the OPCW, Mohammad Katoub, announced that operations to destroy remnants of the Assad-era chemical program have begun, while warning that Israeli attacks hinder the process and that a timeframe for completion has not yet been set.

Syria's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Mohammad Katoub, stated that his country continues full cooperation with the organisation's Technical Secretariat to completely eliminate remnants of the chemical weapons program from the Assad era.
He confirmed that destruction operations have already begun, describing this as tangible progress in the capabilities of Syria's national teams working on this sensitive file.
The announcement falls within an internationally monitored process overseen by the OPCW, the body responsible for verifying the elimination of banned weapons programs.
Ongoing work includes verification, inspection, and destruction of remaining materials and facilities linked to the former program.
Katoub pointed out that Israeli attacks constitute a real obstacle to the removal of the chemical program's remnants, imposing security challenges and operational complications on field teams.
In practical terms, these obstacles tie the pace of work to security conditions at the affected sites, making movement, equipment handling, and field coordination more difficult.

Syria has begun ‌destroying the remnants of a clandestine chemical weapons programme created under former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, Syrian and United Nations officials have said.
This includes raw materials and munitions similar to those used in deadly gas attacks during the country’s civil war, diplomats said at the United Nations Security Council on Thursday.

UN High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi ⁠Nakamitsu told a UN Security Council briefing that for the first time since 2014, the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) had verified the destruction of chemical munitions in Syria.
Syria’s new leadership had located ⁠remnants of al-Assad’s chemical weapons programme in May.

Following the finding, Syria had ‌found “one additional chemical weapons production facility, a newly discovered chemical used in the production of nerve agents, and empty chemical munitions”, Nakamitsu said.

Wide shot, United Nations headquarters 03 SEPTEMBER 2026, NEW YORK CITY 2.
Wide shot, Security Council 3.

SOUNDBITE (English) Izumi Nakamitsu, High Representative for Disarmament Affairs: “Following the OPCW deployment in May 2026 that led to the discovery of previously undeclared chemical weapons, the Syrian Arab Republic submitted amendments to its initial declaration in June 2026. The Syrian Arab Republic declared one additional chemical weapons production facility, a newly discovered chemical used in the production of nerve agents, and empty chemical munitions. It also declared two chemical weapons storage facilities, where the newly discovered materials were being stored. In August 2026, a team from the OPCW Technical Secretariat deployed to Syria to conduct an initial inspection to verify the declaration amendment related to one of the newly declared chemical weapons storage facilities.”
Wide shot, Security Council 5.

SOUNDBITE (English) Izumi Nakamitsu, High Representative for Disarmament Affairs: “In August 2026, the OPCW Technical Secretariat deployed a team to the Syrian Arab Republic to conduct an inspection to verify the destruction of Category 3 chemical weapons. During this deployment, an OPCW inspection team conducted Article IV chemical weapons storage facility and destruction facility verification activities. The OPCW verified that inventories matched recent declarations by the Syrian Arab Republic and verified the irreversible destruction of 42 aerial bombs.”

source_propositions.source_text: A stretch of ocean in Clayoquot Sound is being turned into a kelp nursery, as a First Nation, a restoration group and a kelp company try to rebuild an ecosystem under pressure.

The partnership between the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation, Redd Fish Restoration Society and West Coast Kelp has planted more than 4,200 square metres of new kelp habitat since launching in early 2026 in the traditional territory of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation.
“We have grown a lot of kelp,” Emily Fulton, marine program manager for the nonprofit Redd Fish Restoration Society, told Mongabay in a phone interview.
Organisers describe it as the largest kelp restoration project on the West Coast of North America.
The team is growing baby bull kelp and giant kelp on four lines, each 330 metres long, suspended below the water’s surface and away from seafloor predators such as sea urchins.
As the kelp matures, some of it will be removed from the lines and transplanted to sites across Clayoquot Sound to restore degraded kelp forests and seed new ones.

The project has cost almost a quarter of a million Canadian dollars, with funding from sources including the provincial government, the World Wildlife Fund of Canada and the Clayoquot Biosphere Trust.
“That will make things a lot easier for the people doing kelp restoration. Sea otters are like kelp restoration collaborators.”
“The first time is when they laid the lines, and it was exciting to see it start. It was more exciting to go back three months later, and you can actually see the progression.”

“So, to have that balance is what we’re trying to achieve with our territories. It’s really interesting to see that these are the baby steps we need to take to set it back to pre-contact 300 years ago.”

source_propositions.source_text: A community anti-galamsey group chased a fleeing suspect into the Tano River and caught him, as three men were arrested inside a protected forest reserve where local courts lack judges to try them quickly.
When one of three suspected illegal miners spotted members of a community watch committee closing in on him along the Tano River, he made a desperate dash into the water, hoping to swim to safety.
Members of the Jema Anti-Galamsey Advocacy (JAGA) Watch Committee plunged into the river after him and dragged him back to shore, according to MyJoyOnline.

The dramatic chase unfolded on Friday, October 2, 2026, inside the Tano-Boin Forest Reserve, a protected area that has become a flashpoint in Ghana's ongoing struggle against illegal mining, locally known as galamsey.

JAGA, a volunteer community group based in Jema, said its members intercepted the three men as they operated along the riverbank, reportedly catching them with a water-pumping machine and a 'changfang' — a floating mining raft commonly used by illegal miners to dredge riverbeds for gold.
After the arrest, the suspects were taken to the Jema Police Station and later transferred to the District Police Command at Enchi for prosecution.
But the case quickly ran into a familiar obstacle facing Ghana's rural justice system: the Enchi Magistrate and Circuit Courts currently have no substantive judicial officers to hear cases.
As a result, the three men had to be taken further afield to the Asankragwa Magistrate Court, where they were remanded for one week, MyJoyOnline reports.
JAGA praised the Enchi District Police Command, singling out District Commander Chief Superintendent Mensah for ensuring the suspects were brought before a court despite the logistical hurdles.
This is not JAGA's first encounter with illegal miners in the area.
The group pointed to an earlier case involving two Nigerien nationals arrested for allegedly mining in the Jema-Assemkrom Forest Reserve last year.

No date has been given for when the suspects' remand will be reviewed beyond the one week ordered by the Asankragwa court, and it remains unclear when the Enchi courts will receive substantive judicial officers to handle cases locally.

The three were arrested on Friday, October 2, 2026, when members of the Jema Anti-Galamsey Adovacy (JAGA) Watch Committee intercepted them for allegedly mining within the protected forest reserve.
The suspects were reportedly found in possession of a water-pumping machine and a changfang mining raft.
According to JAGA, one of the suspects attempted to escape by swimming across the river but he was pursued by the watch committee and successfully apprehended.
The District and Regional offices of the Forestry Commission at Enchi and Wiawso were immediately informed of the arrest.

Following the arrests, the three suspects were handed over to the Police at the Jema Police Station and later transferred to the District Police Command at Enchi.

source_propositions.source_text: More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds.
In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age.
Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered.
Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified.

We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time.
The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times.
We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth.
These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago.
It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy.

The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found.

Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies.

First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe.
Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again.
Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date.
Their finding has implications for what kind of energetic event creates these bursts.

“What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them. We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof,” said Manisha Caleb of the University of Sydney, lead author on the study published Thursday in the journal Science.
The MeerTRAP team used the MeerKAT telescope to detect the burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.
